claims.text: Rapid quenching of a magnetic high-entropy alloy increases its coercive field relative to conventional slow cooling.
Rapid quenching refines the alloy microstructure and produces a nanocrystalline grain structure.
Conventional slow cooling produces a coarse-grained microstructure in the magnetic high-entropy alloy.
Rapid quenching increases the density of grain boundaries and dislocations.
Grain boundaries and dislocations act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Quench-induced microstructural defects impede domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Impeded domain-wall motion increases the coercive field.
The rapidly quenched sample will have a statistically significantly higher coercive field than the matched slow-cooled sample.
The slow-cooled baseline has fewer domain-wall pinning sites than the rapidly quenched material.
The proposed effect should hold in high-entropy alloys where domain-wall motion dominates magnetization reversal.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase may vary with alloy composition and processing details.
Current evidence supports increased coercivity with enhanced defect density.
The comparison should use identical compositions, ambient-temperature measurements, identical experimental setups, and cooling rate as the only varied processing factor.
